subject: Survival estimation with mark-resight and telemetry

messages.author: f0c4c757f6cbcd73
messages.subject: Survival estimation with mark-resight and telemetry
parts:
Hi all,

              I’m wrapping up a chapter of my dissertation on beaver demography and I stumbled with a couple of details that complicate a bit the modeling of my data.

I want to estimate beaver survival by age, but: 

1)      I have both telemetry data ( recorded twice a month between October and May for 4 years) and mark resight data (recorded 2-3 times during repeated observations at the  beaver colonies between January and March of each year)

2)      Transmitters can only be fitted to juveniles and adults. However, as we were recapturing individuals every year, we fitted transmitters to kits that at time t+1 became juveniles. Likewise, when transmitters stopped working, we were using mark resight (because individuals fitted with transmitters also had the colored eartags we used for mark resight) to assess survival. This means we can have individuals for which we only have mark resight data, individuals for which we had mark resight data and we  later added telemetry, and individuals for which we had both sources of information but only had mark resight when transmitters stopped working.

I was considering  to convert my telemetry data to mark resight events (particularly since I don’t have recordings in the austral winter) with a detection probability of 1 and then estimate p in the usual way for the mark-resight data. I would build a multistate model (as Kery and Schaub 2012 described in chapter 9 ) with three states: radioed animals, non-radioed animals and dead (somewhat similar to what Kery and Schaub proposed under “estimation of movement between two sites”).

 Does this approach make sense? . Any feedback on this will be highly appreciated


Alejandro

messages.author: 312eda23f89ab6c6
messages.subject: AW: Survival estimation with mark-resight and telemetry
parts:
Hi Alejandro,

Your suggested approach makes much sense to me. It is usually beneficial to analyse different data sets jointly that share parameters (survivial in this case). We have used a similar approach in the past, both in a frequentist and a Bayesian setting. The two papers are Buner & Schaub. 2008. How do different releasing techniques affect the survival of re-introduced grey partridges Perdix perdix? Wildlife Biology 14: 26-35, and Homberger et al. 2014. Food unpredictability in early life increases survival of captive grey partridges (Perdix perdix) after release into the wild. Biological Conservation 177: 134-141. The latter is the Bayesian one and there is an appendix to this paper explaining how the model is implemented via a multistate model, see here for the source: www.researchgate.net/profile/Michael_Schaub2/contributions (check for Dataset: HombergerEtAl GPSurvivalAppendices BiolCons 2014)

Best wishes

Michael
